TIMING: 40 s for this slide (all builds together) · 00:00-00:40 on the 23:45 narration clock.

SAY
Good morning. Zava North Homes has 60,000 homes and three legal clocks running. In the next 25 minutes I will show you the size of that challenge in hard numbers, how we analysed it, the product we designed for it and a forecast you can hold us to.

Zava Forward is one accountable workbench for the retrofit programme, with damp, mould and hazard referral built into every decision: every home has an owner, every decision has evidence, and AI does the preparation so your people can make the calls that matter.

My ask is simple and specific: fund the validation gate, then scale. Let me show you why it is worth it.

SOURCES AND CALCULATIONS
Case brief (E01); exercise addendum (E02).

slides.title: 15,600 homes to lift by 2030. Thousands more to keep safe.
slides.notes:
S02 | 15,600 homes to lift by 2030. Thousands more to keep safe.
TIMING: 70 s for this slide (all builds together) · 00:40-01:50 on the 23:45 narration clock.

SAY
Let me put numbers on the challenge. These are national statistics for social housing in England, applied to Zava's 60,000 homes.

Twenty-six per cent of social homes are still below EPC band C. For Zava that is about 15,600 homes that must be lifted by April 2030.

Six per cent of housing association homes have damp. That is about 3,600 homes. And 38 per cent of housing association households say they live with condensation, damp or mould: about 22,800 households who may pick up the phone.

The median landlord logs 53.5 stage-one complaints per 1,000 homes a year. For Zava, about 3,210 complaints, each one a test of whether the organisation knows what is happening in that home.

This is not a backlog you clear with more spreadsheets. It is a flow you have to run.

SOURCES AND CALCULATIONS
EHS 2024-25 Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 (MHCLG, 29 Jan 2026); SRS MEES final-stage impact assessment (DESNZ/MHCLG, 1 Apr 2026); Tenant Satisfaction Measures 2024/25 headline report (RSH, 4 Nov 2025). Calculation: rate × 60,000, rounded.

S03 | Three clocks are already running.
TIMING: 70 s for this slide (all builds together) · 01:50-03:00 on the 23:45 narration clock.

SAY
Three regulatory clocks are already running, and they converge on the same homes.

First, Awaab's Law. Since 27 October 2025, social landlords must make emergency hazards safe within 24 hours and investigate significant damp and mould within 10 working days, with a written summary to the tenant within three working days.

Second, on 30 November 2026, five weeks from now, phase two adds excess cold and heat, falls, fire and electrical hazards. From that day a cold, inefficient home is a legal hazard, not just a carbon statistic. Retrofit and repairs become one programme.

Third, the government decided on 28 January 2026 that every social rented home must reach EPC band C by 1 April 2030, with a 10,000 pound spend cap per home. And from 2035 a new Decent Homes Standard applies, which on the government's own modelling 42 per cent of housing association homes would fail today.

Every one of these clocks needs the same thing: knowing the state of each home, who owns the next action and what evidence supports it.

SOURCES AND CALCULATIONS
Awaab's Law guidance for social landlords (MHCLG, updated 16 Jul 2026); Awaab's Law collection (MHCLG, 13 Jul 2026); Improving the energy efficiency of socially rented homes: government response (MHCLG/DESNZ, 1 Apr 2026) and summary of responses (28 Jan 2026); New Decent Homes Standard policy statement and EHS modelling briefing (MHCLG, 28 Jan 2026).

slides.title: Homes don't stall on ambition. They stall between teams.
slides.notes:
S04 | Homes don't stall on ambition. They stall between teams.
TIMING: 50 s for this slide (all builds together) · 03:00-03:50 on the 23:45 narration clock.

SAY
Here is what we found when we walked the journey of a single home. The ambition is there. The money is there. Homes stall in the gaps between teams.

A survey says one thing and the stock record says another. Funding needs evidence the assessor has not signed. The resident has not agreed a date. The contractor finishes, but quality acceptance and handover are separate events. Every gap moves the delay to the next team, and on a dashboard it looks like progress because starts go up.

So we changed the management question. Not how many recommendations did we generate, but how many homes reached an accepted handover, how much effort it took and what is blocked, by whom, right now.

SOURCES AND CALCULATIONS
Exercise addendum and journey atlas (E02, E08); agent-request challenge (E03).

slides.title: We challenged the brief to make it shippable.
slides.notes:
S08 | We challenged the brief to make it shippable.
TIMING: 70 s for this slide (all builds together) · 07:20-08:30 on the 23:45 narration clock.

SAY
The original brief asked for five autonomous AI agents, from stock prioritisation to quality verification, with autonomy up to level four. We took the brief seriously, and that is exactly why we challenged it.

We ran it past nine role instruments. Their verdict was clear: none of the five should run end to end. So we kept all five responsibilities as five bounded assistants on one proposal service.

We also refused the easy story that the spreadsheets are the problem. As our requirements put it, Zava does not have a spreadsheet problem, it has a delivery control problem that spreadsheets make harder to see. The first investment is data ownership and workflow, then AI.

We kept AI, and changed its job: AI prepares, people decide, because consent, safety and money need a named human.

The portal is optional, not rejected. Issue #441 assesses resident self-service to reduce avoidable status calls and protect staff working time. Phone, email, letter and visits stay available. Portal/workflow comes first; any resident-answer assistant is separately gated, human-reviewed and off for routine automation. No benefit has been measured.

SOURCES AND CALCULATIONS
Issue #441, read 23 October 2026: owner-confirmed Option B reuses case/API authority; portal/workflow first, resident-answer task separately gated. Its latest public comment reports a Research-stage integration blocker and no published PR. The owner reports local work in progress, not inspected implementation or approval. Per-message human review remains normative; routine automation stays off pending requirements-owner disposition and separate release approval.
Original case brief: five agents with autonomy L2-L4 (E01); agent-request challenge and agent what-if study: "none of the five requested agents should be end-to-end" (E03, WIS); BRD L161-166 spreadsheet quote; discovery brief: first investment is data ownership and workflow instrumentation; PRD: one proposal service, not five applications; architecture README: no resident portal required, separate workers deferred, Foundry Agent Service not used.

S09 | Every prototype taught us something we kept.
TIMING: 50 s for this slide (all builds together) · 08:30-09:20 on the 23:45 narration clock.

SAY
We did not design this on a whiteboard. Every prototype taught us something we kept.

It started on 20 September with a review of the open decisions in the requirements. The first prototype gave each role its own perspective, and taught us that roles need their own queues. On 6 October we reviewed eleven perspectives, nine workflow filters and eight constructed cases, found inconsistent owner labels, and fixed them in the requirements. Two days later the MVP replaced the prototype with one shared workbench.

On 11 October we made real AI, Azure SQL and Blob storage mandatory, and the decision-model and generative calls worked. By 14 October five assistants were making real, citation-validated proposals backed by 73 SQL tests, and the evidence survived a service restart. This morning we merged the Tokenomics requirements: AI is managed by cost per accepted outcome.

Twenty-five days from the first prototype review to five real assistants. Every lesson became a requirement, a decision or a test.

slides.title: Meet the Workbench: every home, one owner, one next step.
slides.notes:
S11 | Meet the Workbench: every home, one owner, one next step.
TIMING: 70 s for this slide (all builds together) · 10:30-11:40 on the 23:45 narration clock.

SAY
This is the product. We call it the Workbench, and it is deliberately simple.

Every person opens to their cases. Every case shows one next owner, a plain status and the evidence behind it. When two sources disagree, the case does not disappear into an amber dot: it goes to the person who can resolve it, with the clock visible.

AI sits in the side panel. It prepares a summary, a letter or a funding pack, and a person accepts it or rejects it with a reason. Nothing is approved by a model.
